title: Traverse a linked list (start from head, follow next pointers until null, print each node's data).

s1_definition.profdef: Traversing a linked list means visiting every node exactly once by starting at the head and following each node's next reference until you reach null. You use a moving pointer, usually called `current`, process each node's data, then advance `current` to `current.next`. It is O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India keeps Rajesh's pending transaction slips as a chain, each pointing to the next. To total them up, a clerk starts at the first slip, reads it, follows its arrow to the next slip, reads that, and keeps going until a slip's arrow points to nothing. At that point every slip has been read exactly once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Start at the head, process each node, follow next, and stop when you reach null.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Traversing a linked list means visiting every node exactly once by starting at the head and following each node's next reference until you reach null. You use a moving pointer, usually called `current`, process each node's data, then advance `current` to `current.next`. It is O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India keeps Rajesh's pending transaction slips as a chain, each pointing to the next. To total them up, a clerk starts at the first slip, reads it, follows its arrow to the next slip, reads that, and keeps going until a slip's arrow points to nothing. At that point every slip has been read exactly once.

**One line to remember:** Start at the head, process each node, follow next, and stop when you reach null.

sections.s2_technical:
Traversal is the most fundamental linked-list operation and underlies searching, counting, summing, and printing. You declare a local pointer `current` and set it to `head`. You then loop while `current` is not null: inside the loop you do whatever work you need with `current`'s data, and at the end of each iteration you advance with `current = current.next`. When `current` becomes null you have passed the last node and the loop ends.

A critical rule is never to move `head` itself during traversal, because `head` must keep pointing at the first node. If you accidentally reassigned `head` to `head.next` repeatedly, you would lose the start of the list and could not use it again. That is why you always traverse with a separate `current` pointer and leave `head` untouched.

Traversal visits each node once, so it is O(n) time, and it uses only one extra pointer regardless of list length, so it is O(1) space. You can traverse to accumulate a value, such as summing transaction amounts into a BigDecimal, or to find a node matching a condition. For a doubly linked list you could traverse backwards from the tail using previous references, but the forward singly linked traversal is the canonical pattern.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India needs to compute the total of all of Rajesh's pending transactions, which are stored as a linked chain. The system must visit every node and add its amount. This is exactly how traversal works — walk from head to null, processing each node.

Problem 2 — The traversal must not damage the list, because the pending chain is needed again later for processing. This is exactly why we traverse with a separate current pointer and never move head.

The code has a `TransactionNode` and a `PendingLedger` class with a `total` method that traverses and sums, plus a `printAll` method. The demo builds a chain and totals it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a chain built by appending 1000, 2000, 3000, so head points to 1000, which points to 2000, which points to 3000, which points to null.

Step 1 — total starts sum at 0 and sets current to head (the 1000 node).

Step 2 — current is not null, so add 1000: sum is 1000. Advance current to the 2000 node.

Step 3 — current is not null, so add 2000: sum is 3000. Advance current to the 3000 node.

Step 4 — current is not null, so add 3000: sum is 6000. Advance current to null.

Step 5 — current is null, loop ends. Return 6000. Throughout, head still points at the 1000 node, so the list is intact and can be reused.

```

2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO]   Rs.1000.00
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO]   Rs.2000.00
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO]   Rs.3000.00
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Total pending = Rs.6000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Chain: head → [1000] → [2000] → [3000] → null
    │
    ▼
  PendingLedger.total()
    │ current=head  sum=0
    │ 1000 → sum=1000   current→2000
    │ 2000 → sum=3000   current→3000
    │ 3000 → sum=6000   current→null → stop
    ▼
  return 6000   (head unchanged, list reusable)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Traversing a linked list means visiting every node exactly once by starting at the head and following each node's next reference until I reach null. I use a local pointer, which I usually call current, set it to the head, and loop while it is not null. Inside the loop I do whatever work I need with the current node's data, and at the end of each iteration I advance current to current dot next. When current becomes null I have gone past the last node and the loop ends. Traversal visits each node once, so it is linear time, and I use only a single extra pointer, so it is constant space.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used traversal to total up Rajesh's pending transactions, which are stored as a linked chain. I walk from the head to the end, adding each node's BigDecimal amount into a running sum, and return the total.

The rule I always stress is that I traverse with a separate current pointer and never move the head itself. The head must keep pointing at the first node, because the pending chain is needed again later for actual processing. If I carelessly advanced the head instead of a separate pointer, I would lose the start of the list after one traversal and could never walk it again. That discipline of leaving the head untouched and moving only a local pointer is what keeps the list safe and reusable.
